title: Chips, power and water
essentialQuestion: What does AI need from the planet, and who pays for it?
learningGoal: Explain what AI data centres need from the planet, and weigh their benefits and costs for the places where they are built.

warmUp.question: When you ask an AI tool a question, where do you think the answer is made?
options: In a big building far away

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: What does each person hope for? What does each person worry about?

cards.title: A data centre is coming to Coralton

cases.name: The data centre company
cases.body: “We will build a huge building full of computers that run AI tools. About 1,000 people will help to build it over two years. About 50 people will work there after it opens, and we will train local young people for some of those jobs. We will put solar panels on the roof.”

cases.name: Hana, who runs a small fish farm
cases.body: “My fish need clean water and power all day and all night. I worry that the data centre will use the town's water in the dry season, and that power cuts will get longer.”

cases.name: Leo, a young electrician
cases.body: “I hope to get work on the building site and learn new skills. Two years of work would help me a lot.”

cases.name: The town's water office
cases.body: “In the dry season, the river is low. The data centre needs water to cool its computers. It could use cleaned waste water instead of river water.”

cases.name: A member of the town council
cases.body: “The company will bring money to Coralton. But most people who use its AI tools live in other countries.”

activity.title: Benefit or cost?
activity.instructions: Put each sentence about the Coralton data centre into a group. There is no score. After you place one, you can see one possible answer and the reason.

items.text: About 1,000 people get building work for two years.
items.feedback: People earn money and learn skills, but the work ends when the building is finished. So you could also say both.

items.text: About 50 people get long-term jobs inside.
items.feedback: Any group can be right here. Long-term jobs help, but 50 is a small number for such a huge building.

items.text: The data centre uses as much power as a small city.
items.feedback: The town must share its power. Making more power may mean more pollution.

items.text: It takes river water to cool its computers.
items.feedback: In the dry season, there may be less water for farms and homes.

items.text: The company puts solar panels on the roof.
items.feedback: Power from the sun is clean, so the data centre takes less power from the town.

items.text: It cleans waste water and uses it for cooling.
items.feedback: The river water stays for farms and homes.

items.text: A big company from abroad brings money to the town.
items.feedback: Any group can be right here. New money can help the town grow. But much of what the company earns may go to other countries.

items.text: The company trains local young people to work inside.
items.feedback: People learn skills they can use in other jobs too. If only a few get places, you could also say both.

activity.saves: The group the learner chose for each sentence, with the lesson's other answers.
activity.offline: Everything is in the lesson file. Nothing is sent anywhere.

sections.heading: AI runs in big buildings full of chips
sections.text: When you ask an AI tool a question, your device usually doesn't make the answer itself. Some small tools can. But most of the time, the question travels to a data centre, a large building full of computers. Inside are thousands of chips that do trillions of sums every second. They use a lot of electricity and get very hot, so many data centres use water to cool them. An international energy agency estimated that in 2024, all the world's data centres used about 1.5% of its electricity. Only part of that was for AI. Data centres also run websites, videos and messages. The agency expects data centres to use about twice as much by 2030, mostly because of AI. That is a forecast, not a measurement.
sections.simpler: Usually, an AI answer is not made in your device. Some small tools do work on a phone. But most questions go to a data centre, a big building full of computers. Its chips do huge amounts of maths. They use a lot of power and get very hot. Water often helps to cool them. In 2024, all data centres used about 1.5% of the world's power. Only part was for AI. Experts think this may double by 2030, mostly because of AI. That is a forecast.

sections.heading: Chips need minerals and a few factories
sections.text: Chips are made from materials dug out of the ground. Some need rare minerals, which are often mined in ways that harm nature. Very few factories can make the most powerful chips. In 2021, a chip industry study found that most of the world's most advanced chips were made in one place, Taiwan. So a problem in one place could cause chip shortages around the world. Old chips and computers also become electronic waste. This waste can contain harmful metals, such as mercury and lead.
sections.simpler: Chips are made from things dug out of the ground. Some need rare minerals. Digging them up can harm nature. Only a few factories make the best chips. In 2021, a study found most are made in Taiwan. A problem there could slow chips everywhere. Old computers become waste. Some of it is harmful.

sections.heading: Who gains, and who pays?
sections.text: Data centres are being built fast in Southeast Asia. Singapore paused new ones in 2019, and in 2021 they used about 7% of its electricity. Many companies then built in Johor, in Malaysia, and on Batam, in Indonesia. Data centres bring investment, building work that ends when the building is finished, and some long-term jobs. Malaysia's government hopes they will help to modernise its economy. But critics say they create far fewer jobs than they promise. Many of their users live in other countries. Some people nearby worry about water shortages and power cuts. Companies can lower these costs with more efficient AI, power from the sun and wind, and cleaned, reused water.
sections.simpler: Singapore paused new data centres in 2019. So companies built in Johor, Malaysia, and Batam, Indonesia. Data centres bring investment. They bring building work for a few years, and some long-term jobs. Malaysia hopes they will help it grow richer. But some people say they bring fewer jobs than promised. Many users live in other countries. People nearby worry about water and power cuts. Companies can make AI more efficient. They can use sun and wind power, and clean and reuse water.

glossary.definition: A large building full of computers that store and process information.
glossary.example: The new data centre in Coralton will run AI tools.

glossary.definition: A tiny part inside a computer that does its sums.
glossary.example: The data centre has thousands of chips, and they get very hot.

glossary.definition: A natural material that people dig out of the ground.
Money a company spends in a place, hoping to earn more later.
glossary.example: The data centre is a big investment in Coralton.

glossary.definition: Doing a job well while using less power, water or time.
glossary.example: A more efficient data centre uses less electricity for the same work.

checks.question: Why do many data centres use water?

options.text: To make electricity for the town
options.feedback: Not quite. Data centres use electricity. Read about the hot chips in the first section.

options.text: To wash the computers each day
options.feedback: Not quite. The water is not for washing. Read about the hot chips in the first section.

options.text: To cool chips that get very hot
options.feedback: Yes. The chips do so much work that they get very hot, so water helps to cool them.

checks.question: What happens to the building work at a data centre?

options.text: It lasts as long as the data centre runs
options.feedback: Not quite. Building work is for building it. Read the third section.

options.text: It ends when the building is finished
options.feedback: Yes. Many people build it for a few years. In Coralton, about 50 people will work there after it opens.

options.text: It is done by computers, not people
options.feedback: Not quite. People build data centres. Read the third section.

checks.question: What promise would you ask the data centre company to make?
checks.placeholder: I would ask the company to promise ... because ...

write.prompt: Should Coralton say yes to the data centre? Give your answer, one benefit, one cost, and one promise you would ask the company to make.
sentenceStarters: I would ask the company to promise ...
selfCheck: I said yes, no or yes with a promise.
I gave one benefit and one cost.
I gave one promise the company should make.
write.example: I think Coralton should say yes, but only with a promise. One benefit is that about 1,000 people get building work for two years, and people like Leo can learn new skills. One cost is that the data centre needs a lot of water to cool its chips. In the dry season, Hana's fish farm and the town's homes could get less. I would ask the company to promise to use cleaned waste water, not river water. This matters because the town needs water more than the AI tools do.

speak.partnerTask: Your partner says one benefit of the Coralton data centre. You say one cost. Then switch.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud three things a data centre needs to work. Then say who might pay for them.

watch.title: Why are AI data centers using so much electricity? - Sajan Saini
watch.why: A short animated lesson shows what is inside an AI data centre, why it gets so hot, and asks how much of the planet's resources AI should use.
watch.beforeQuestion: What do you think is inside an AI data centre?
watch.afterQuestion: What two ways does the video give to make AI use less energy?
watch.summary: Since 2019, more than a thousand huge AI data centres have been built around the world. Each one can use as much water as a small town. It can use as much electricity as a small city. Inside, there are thousands of racks of computers with special chips. These chips do trillions of sums every second, to answer questions and to train AI. All this work makes the chips very hot. Engineers cool them with water towers, cold water in pipes, or special liquids. They also send data with light instead of copper wires, which wastes less power. But AI tools keep getting bigger, so they need more and more electricity. The video asks if we could build smaller tools for smaller jobs. It ends with a question: how much of the planet's resources should we use for smarter machines?
keyPoints: AI data centres use huge amounts of electricity and water.
Chips get very hot, so engineers look for new ways to cool them and save power.
People must decide how much of the planet's resources AI should use.
watch.contentNote: About 6 minutes (6:16), an animated TED-Ed lesson by Sajan Saini, released in September 2026, with fast American English. The title and channel were confirmed with YouTube's oEmbed on 31 October 2026, and the length is from TED's page for the lesson. The summary was written from the transcript on TED's website (https://www.ted.com/talks/sajan_saini_why_are_ai_data_centers_using_so_much_electricity), not from watching it. It names two AI tools (Claude and ChatGPT), uses US examples (New York City), and mentions companies planning their own nuclear power plants. Its numbers (for example, enough energy for 300,000 homes) are the video's own and are not repeated in the lesson. Someone on the team must watch it before use; learners can read the written summary instead.

visual.description: PLACEHOLDER: no picture exists yet, and visuals/DW06.svg is only a planned path. A left-to-right chain of four simple drawings joined by arrows: a mine with a pile of rocks (“Minerals from the ground”), a factory (“Chip factory”), a large windowless building (“Data centre”), and a tablet showing an answer (“Your answer”). Into the data centre run a power line labelled “Electricity” and a water pipe labelled “Water for cooling”; out of its roof rise wavy lines labelled “Heat”. Under the data centre, two small labels: “Benefit: jobs and investment” and “Cost: power and water for the town”. Words carry every meaning; no real logos or company names.
visual.alt: A chain from a mine to a chip factory, a data centre and a tablet. Electricity and water flow into the data centre, and heat comes out.

sources.label: Scientific American, from Nature (10 April 2025): Data centers will use twice as much energy by 2030, driven by AI (reporting the International Energy Agency's Energy and AI report: all data centres, 2024 estimate and 2030 projection)
Apple (2024): Apple Intelligence Foundation Language Models (a small model that runs on the device, and a larger one on servers)
UN Environment Programme (21 September 2024): AI has an environmental problem. Here's what the world can do about that.
Reuters, via Malay Mail (1 April 2021): Global chip supply chain increasingly vulnerable to massive disruption, study finds (Semiconductor Industry Association)
Associated Press, via The Star (19 February 2025): Malaysia is betting on data centers to boost its economy. But experts warn they come at a price.
Kontinentalist (2026): Thirsty, tired, wired: Singapore, Johor, Batam and the data centre boom

sensitiveNotes: Power cuts, water shortages and the cost of electricity may be part of learners' daily lives. Don't ask about their homes, bills or access to water and power; keep the discussion on Coralton and the reported facts. Some learners may live in or near the places named (Johor, Batam, Singapore): keep it neutral, about choices every town faces, not blame for any country or its people.
educatorNotes: The numbers are dated and scoped. Electricity: the International Energy Agency's Energy and AI report (April 2025), as reported by Scientific American and Nature, estimated that all data centres used about 415 TWh in 2024, about 1.5% of the world's electricity, and projected about 945 TWh by 2030, roughly what Japan uses in a year now. The 1.5% is for all data centres, not AI alone: the IEA estimated that AI servers were about 15% of data-centre energy use in 2024, and one outside researcher thinks that is an underestimate. The 2030 figure is a projection with stated uncertainty, not a measurement. (The IEA's own pages could not be opened on 1 November 2026; check them, and its later Key questions on energy and AI, if you can.) On the device: some small models run on phones and laptops (for example Apple's roughly 3-billion-parameter model, 2024), while most large tools run in data centres. Taiwan's share of the most advanced chip-making (92%) is from a 2021 Semiconductor Industry Association study. Singapore paused new data centres in 2019; in 2021 they used about 7% of its electricity (Kontinentalist). The earlier draft's “30 to 50 long-term jobs” (Good Jobs First, via AP, scope not stated) and UNEP's “800 kg of materials for a 2 kg computer” (no source given) were removed. The fish farmer in the AP story worried about longer power cuts, like Hana.

Rules for data centres in Johor and Batam change quickly (in early 2026, after residents protested about water, Malaysia stopped new applications for non-AI data centres in Johor and tightened water approvals, Kontinentalist reports). Check the latest news before teaching the third section. Data centres also run websites, videos and messages, not only AI. Benefits are real too: investment (AP reports over US$31 billion for Malaysia in the first 10 months of 2024, from Knight Frank), building work and some long-term jobs; UNEP also notes that AI can help to monitor the environment. Some places give data centres large tax breaks, so ask who gains from a deal.

Paper version of the activity: write the eight sentences on cards and sort them into Benefit, Cost and Both. There is no score; reward reasons, and accept a different group with a good reason. A partner could swap Coralton for a short, neutral local example, such as a new factory or mine. The claim record is in content/courses/digital-world/claims/DW06.md.

Revised on 1 November 2026 from Justin's review: both readings now say the answer is usually made in a data centre and that some small tools run on the device; the 1.5% is described as all data centres in 2024 (the IEA's 2025 report), with only part of it for AI, and the 2030 doubling as a forecast; building work (temporary) is separated from long-term jobs; the unsourced “most give only 30 to 50 jobs” (and its quick check) and UNEP's unsourced 800 kg figure were removed; Singapore's 7% is now dated 2021; Malaysia's hopes and the investment are added as local benefits, and Coralton's company now trains local young people (a new activity item replaces Hana's power-cut item, which the electricity item covers). Coralton stays fictional and labelled; real sources are in the reading and teacher notes, not mixed into the evidence. Activity feedback gives reasons without “Most people would say” and accepts other groups where a reason fits. Six sources (one over the checker's aim) because the on-device point needed its own.
